title: The Kitty Genovese Story
summary: True crime episode on the 1964 murder of Catherine "Kitty" Genovese in Kew Gardens, Queens, and its aftermath. Covers her background and personal life, the March 13, 1964 attack by Winston Moseley, the witnesses who heard or saw parts of it, the New York Times article "37 Who Saw Murder Didn't Call the Police" and its later criticism in 2004, the bystander effect research it inspired, Moseley's later crimes, escape, prison life, and parole denials, and a listener mail follow-up on fish fraud and marine fisheries observers.

segments.title: Intro and San Francisco tour plug
segments.summary: Josh plugs a San Francisco Sketch Fest show, then the hosts introduce the episode as a true crime installment about Kitty Genovese and discuss why her story is well known and how the documentary The Witness revived her story.

segments.title: Kitty Genovese's early life and family
segments.summary: Born in Brooklyn to Italian American parents, Kitty was popular in school and had a close bond with her younger brother Bill. The family moved to New Canaan, Connecticut after she graduated high school, while she stayed in New York. She briefly married a man named Rocco, worked as a bar manager in Hollis, Queens, and met Mary Ann Zlonkay in 1963 at a lesbian bar in the Village.

segments.title: The March 1964 attack
segments.summary: On March 13, 1964, around 3:15 a.m., Winston Moseley followed Kitty home from her bar job in Kew Gardens. He stabbed her outside a bookstore, she screamed, and Robert Mozer opened his window and yelled, driving him off. Moseley returned about thirty minutes later, found her in the vestibule of her building, and killed her. Carl Ross heard and saw from his door and did not act.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Short break before the discussion of the witnesses; no ad content recorded beyond the transition.

segments.title: Witnesses and the New York Times article
segments.summary: Neighbor Sophia Farrar went down and stayed with Kitty as she died. The New York Times ran a short story, then after a police commissioner's comment, A.M. Rosenthal assigned Martin Gansberg to write the front-page story titled '37 Who Saw Murder Didn't Call the Police.' The article overstated what witnesses saw; in 2004 the Times revisited the case, and the hosts discuss the errors and the fact that Farrar was omitted.

segments.title: Bystander effect and its legacy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the story led to research on bystander apathy and the psychology of crowds, diffusion of responsibility, and social influence, and how the case shaped the image of Queens and urban indifference. They disagree on how much blame the witnesses deserve.

segments.title: Winston Moseley's later crimes and prison life
segments.summary: A week later Moseley was caught burglarizing a house in another neighborhood and held by a neighbor until police arrived. He confessed to Genovese and other murders, was sentenced to death, then resentenced to life. He escaped in Buffalo while being taken to a hospital from Attica, held hostages, and was returned to prison. He was later involved in the Attica riots. He was denied parole eighteen times and died in prison in 2016. Bill Genovese's attempt to interview him was refused.

segments.title: The Witness documentary and Moseley's son
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Bill Genovese's search for closure in The Witness, including his meeting with one of Moseley's sons and the differing views on how that conversation went. They also note that Joseph Fink and Carl Ross are the two witnesses still faulted.

segments.title: Listener mail: fish fraud follow-up
segments.summary: A listener who works as a marine fisheries observer in the Bering Sea writes about observer programs on fishing vessels, which the hosts had covered in their fish fraud episode.
